whyItExists.short: article and section give semantic meaning to content blocks — distinguishing self-contained pieces from grouped sub-sections.
whyItExists.problem: div has no meaning. When a page has many content blocks wrapped in divs, nothing tells search engines or screen readers what each block represents.
whyItExists.solution: article marks self-contained, redistributable content (a blog post, a product card, a tweet). section marks a thematic grouping within a larger piece of content.
whyItExists.impact: Search engines use article to identify the main content body for indexing. RSS readers and scrapers use it to extract article text automatically.

explainModes.beginner: article is for content that makes sense on its own — like a blog post. section is for grouping related parts within a page. div is just a box with no meaning.
explainModes.simple: Use article when content could be published or shared independently (a news story, a product). Use section to divide a page into themed groups. Use div only when you need a container for layout/styling with no semantic meaning.
explainModes.standard: article implies the content is self-contained and could be syndicated. section implies a thematic grouping that belongs to the larger document — it should always have a heading. div has no semantic meaning and should be used last. They can nest: an article can contain sections; a section can contain articles.
explainModes.technical: Both article and section are sectioning content elements — they create new scopes for heading outlines. article has an implicit ARIA role of `article`. section has role `region` only when it has an accessible name (aria-label or aria-labelledby). Without a name, section is treated as a generic element. div always has role `generic`.
explainModes.deepDive: The HTML5 document outline algorithm (now abandoned) tried to allow multiple h1 elements inside sectioning elements. Modern browsers and screen readers never implemented it. The practical rule: treat each sectioning element as if it resets the heading hierarchy for screen readers — always start with a heading directly inside article and section. Google's indexing treats article content as high-quality candidate text for rich results and Featured Snippets.

content.text: Three elements handle content grouping in HTML — each with different intent:

items: **section** — thematic grouping within a document (always add a heading)
**div** — a generic box with no semantic meaning (use as last resort)

content.question: Which element should wrap a blog post that could be shared as a standalone piece of content?
content.explanation: article is for self-contained, independently redistributable content like blog posts, news articles, product cards, or forum posts.

content.question: True or false: A section element should always contain a heading.
content.explanation: section represents a thematic grouping. Without a heading, neither humans nor machines can identify what the group is about. If there's no natural heading, use div instead.

faq.q: Can I put article inside article?
faq.a: Yes. A comments section inside a blog post is a common example — the post is an article, and each comment is a nested article.

faq.q: What is the difference between section and div?
faq.a: section has semantic meaning — it groups related content thematically and should have a heading. div is a generic container with no semantic meaning, used purely for layout and styling.

faq.q: Does Google understand article and section?
faq.a: Yes. Google's crawlers parse semantic HTML. article helps identify primary content for Featured Snippets. section helps understand page structure for breadcrumb rich results.

examples: Medium wraps each blog post body in an article element
Twitter/X marks each tweet as an article in the timeline
